title: Why a poem
hookLine: teaching through beauty: he wrote so people would stay for the teaching

cards: A spoonful of honey, and under it, something bitter. It's an old trick with children: the medicine goes down because something sweet goes with it. A monk used the same picture to explain his writing.

At the very end of the poem of Nanda, after all the longing, the journey and the letting go, Ashvaghosha steps out from behind the story and talks to the reader directly. He explains why a monk would write poetry at all.

teach.b: First, the purpose. He says the poem is about liberation, and that he wrote it not to give pleasure but to bring calm. The beauty was never the point.

teach.h: FOR MINDS SET ON OTHER THINGS.
teach.b: He wrote in this ornate style, he says, to catch listeners whose minds are on other things.
People who would never sit through a plain teaching might sit through a love affair, a king, a heavenly journey, and stay long enough to hear what it was really about. Third, the honey.
Then the picture: just as bitter medicine is mixed with honey so it can be swallowed, he has mixed the teaching with poetry. Whatever in the poem is about liberation is the medicine.
The rest, the descriptions, the music of the verse, is there to help it go down. Fourth, the gold.

teach.h: KEEP THE GOLD, LET THE DUST GO.
teach.b: He asks readers to take what leads to peace and leave the rest, the way someone panning for gold keeps the gold and lets the dust wash away. So the honey is honest about being honey. He isn't hiding the teaching.
He's telling you exactly where it is. He said this about the poem of Nanda, but hold the same idea up to the life we've heard these weeks.
The empty saddle, the birds in one tree for a night, the dog with a dry bone, the torch of straw. Each one is honey around something hard: parting, grief, craving, and the way out.
The poet hoped his listeners would stay for the beauty, and then keep the gold.

how: Buddhist communities also teach through story, verse and art: temple murals of the Buddha's life, chanted verses, and retellings of the birth stories, often alongside plain instruction in the teaching.

games.q: the poet's reasons: tap the pairs.

s: Ashvaghosha wrote poetry mainly to entertain
he says he wrote not for pleasure but for calm.
he compares his poem to medicine mixed with honey
the teaching is the medicine; the verse helps it go down.
he hides the teaching so readers won't notice it
he tells readers plainly to keep what leads to peace and leave the rest.

games.q: you have a teaching that can free people, but most of your listeners would rather hear a love story. what do you do?
o: teach it plainly; whoever leaves, leaves.
wrap the teaching inside a beautiful story, and say so.
games.why: Ashvaghosha mixes the teaching with poetry like medicine with honey, then tells readers to keep the gold and let the dust go.

practice: Find something beautiful within reach, light on a wall, a sound outside, the color of a cup, and take it in fully for a few breaths. Then, without forcing an answer, ask gently what it might be carrying, and rest in whatever comes.

wordCard.voice: Honey. The image Ashvaghosha used for his poetry: medicine mixed with honey, so the teaching can go down easily. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: beauty carries it. The verse is the honey; the teaching is the medicine. Day seven hundred twenty-three, done.
